chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Isma'il ibn Marar from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from some of his men from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the threshold of the traveler who fasts and completes [the prayer], he said: 'Any traveler who stays in his house or in the town he enters for less than the stay of ten days, fasting and completion [of prayer] are obligatory upon him always, and if his stay in his house or in the town he enters is more than ten days, then shortening [of prayer] and breaking the fast are upon him.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And whoever whose journey is an act of disobedience to Allah, or for leisurely hunting or for arrogance, or who is following a tyrannical ruler, then completion [of prayer] is upon him.' (640) 15 This is indicated by what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Ammar ibn Marwan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'I heard him say:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting and prayer for a traveler who stays in one place for more or less than ten days?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib* clarifies the ten-day threshold for the traveler's status, distinguishing between the obligation to fast (for stays under ten days) and the permission to break fast and shorten prayers (for stays exceeding ten days). It further refines the general rule by specifying that journeys for *ma'siyah* (disobedience), such as hunting for sport or following a tyrant, negate the concession, requiring full observance regardless of duration. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the spiritual intent and context of the journey alongside its physical duration.
